parts.title: 1.1 — The Human Terrain of Strategy Execution
content: Strategy enters an organisation through the people responsible for interpreting and acting on it. Before strategy becomes operational activity, it passes through two human filters:
Cognition — Mind
How individuals interpret what strategy means. Shaped by professional expertise, mental shortcuts, past experience, and risk perception.
Emotion — Heart
How individuals experience the strategy. Shapes engagement energy, morale, friction load, psychological safety, and values alignment.
The Result
Whether strategy produces clarity or confusion, commitment or compliance. Execution begins inside the human system.

The deeper challenge behind execution friction: Strategy is fundamentally a human interpretation problem. The Functional Bias Problem reveals that when perspectives diverge, even highly capable executives can unintentionally pull the organisation in different directions.
✎ Reflection
In your current role, which filter (Mind or Heart) tends to shape your first response to a new strategic priority? What are the implications?
prompts: ✎ Reflection In your current role, which filter (Mind or Heart) tends to shape your first response to a new strategic priority? What are the implications?

parts.title: 1.2 — The Five Principles of Aligning Heart & Mind
content: Principle 1
Strategy Moves Through People
The human entry point of execution. Alignment of the mind (cognition) and heart (emotion) is the first execution system.

Cognitive alignment focuses on making biases visible so they can be managed deliberately. Emotional alignment requires naming the current state through which strategy is being experienced. Leaders operating from Joy, Commitment, and Confidence invest very differently from those operating from Fear, Uncertainty, or Disengagement.
➤ Insight: Can you name the dominant emotion your team is carrying into the current strategy? If you cannot name it, you cannot manage it.
Principle 2
Misalignment Fragments Effort

When interpretation and emotional experience diverge, effort begins to fragment. The three most visible consequences: Chinese Whispers (intent mutates downward), Clarification Debt (leadership time consumed by re-explanation), Silent Disengagement (compliance without commitment).
Data: Low-alignment organisations experience 41% lower productivity and 48% higher turnover (Gallup; PMI). This drift is gradual, rationalised, and expensive.
Principle 3
Alignment Must Be Designed

Alignment rarely emerges naturally. It must be intentionally designed. Two diagnostic assessments support this: the OCEAVL Assessment (surfaces psychological tendencies influencing decision-making) and the Emotional Climate Assessment (identifies the prevailing state of being through which strategy is currently being experienced). Both available on demand.
➤ Insight: These assessments are leadership mirrors. Their power lies in the conversation they generate.
Principle 4
Human Reactions Are Predictable

Reactions to strategic change follow predictable psychological patterns. The SCARF Model explains five social conditions that trigger emotional responses during change. The human brain processes social change using the same threat circuitry as physical danger — any new goal, system, or way of working is evaluated emotionally before it is evaluated rationally.
➤ Insight: When you can name which SCARF trigger is driving resistance, you can address the root cause.
Principle 5
Execution Must Be Visible in Behaviour

Without observable behaviour, alignment remains theoretical. The ACE-IT Framework defines five universally desired behaviours: Accountability, Commitment, Engagement, Integrity, Transparency — independent of an organisation’s stated values. They represent the minimum behavioural standard for any leadership team serious about execution.
➤ Insight: If someone external observed your team for one week, which ACE-IT behaviour would they see most clearly? Which would be absent?
✎ Reflection
Which of the Five Principles describes the most critical gap in your leadership team right now? What is the evidence for this?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Which of the Five Principles describes the most critical gap in your leadership team right now? What is the evidence for this?

parts.title: 1.3 — Change Management: The 4 Checks of Mind, Heart, Hands and Habit
content: 1.1 showed that strategy reaches people through two filters, Mind and Heart. 1.2 showed that alignment has to be designed. This part applies both to the moment a strategy asks people to work differently.
Change management is the leadership discipline of moving people from current practice to the practice the strategy requires.
The event and the transition

A change is an event. It is announced on a date, and on that date the structure, the system or the target is different. The transition is what each affected person goes through afterwards: letting go of a familiar practice, working out what the new one asks of them, and becoming able to do it. The event belongs to the organisation. The transition belongs to the person.

A leadership team debates a change for months before announcing it. Leaders finish their own transition on the day everyone else begins theirs. The distance between the two is where impatience on one side meets resistance on the other. Change management is the work of leading people across that distance.
The 4 Checks of Mind, Heart, Hands and Habit

A change is adopted when it passes four checks for the people it affects. Mind and Heart are the two filters from 1.1. Hands and Habit extend the same path to the point where the new practice is real. Each check asks one question and has one tool. Expand each check.
Check 1 · Mind
They understand the change, why it matters and what they do differently.

Understanding is tested by what people can say back in their own words. An announcement shows that the leader has spoken. The check shows what the people have understood, after each of them has passed the message through their own expertise, shortcuts, experience and sense of risk.
Tool: the 3S Check (1.4).
✓ Passed when: people in the same team describe the change in the same way.
⚠ Failed when: people repeat the slogan and cannot say what they personally do differently.
Check 2 · Heart
They want it to succeed.

Wanting is a decision each person makes. It is the ignition point described in Section 2: “This matters to me.” Most changes threaten something for the people they touch: standing, certainty, control, belonging or fairness. Until that threat is addressed, a person who understands the change holds back their energy.
Tool: the SCARF Model (1.5).
✓ Passed when: people bring problems and ideas to the change.
⚠ Failed when: the room is quiet, effort is minimal and people say they are “waiting for alignment”.
Check 3 · Hands
They are able to do it.

Ability is practical. It rests on four things: skill, time, authority and tools. A person can understand a change and want it, and still be unable to do it on an ordinary working day. From a distance, that person looks the same as one who is unwilling.
Tool: the STAT Check (1.6).
✓ Passed when: people do the new work unaided.
⚠ Failed when: workarounds appear, decisions are passed upward and the new practice is done last.
Check 4 · Habit
It has become the way they work.

A practice becomes habit when it is repeated, noticed and expected. Until then it depends on effort and attention, and both fall away under pressure. The five ACE-IT behaviours are what hold a new practice in place after the launch has passed.
Tool: ACE-IT (1.7).
✓ Passed when: the practice holds when the leader is absent.
⚠ Failed when: the old way returns under the first pressure.
Why the order matters

Each check depends on the one before it. A person cannot want a change they have misread. They will not perform a change they do not want, and skill offered to an unwilling person is left unused. A practice cannot become habit while most people are unable to perform it.
The practical rule follows. A change stalls at the first check it fails, and that check is where the leader’s effort belongs. Effort spent further along the path is lost.
A team that understands a change and resents it has stalled at Heart. More explanation will not move it.
A team that wants a change and has no authority to act has stalled at Hands. More encouragement will not move it.
A team that did it well for a month and drifted back has stalled at Habit. A relaunch will not hold it.
The leader’s four jobs
Leading the transition means doing one job at each check. Each job is taught with its tool in the four parts that follow.
Check | Tool | Leader’s job | Complete when
Mind | 3S | Explain | Three people from the affected group give the same Shift, Stake and Step.
Heart | SCARF | Involve | The people affected can point to a part of the change they shaped.
Hands | STAT | Equip | A person can perform the new practice from start to finish without asking permission or using a workaround.
Habit | ACE-IT | Reinforce | The practice holds through a full review period with the leader absent.
Industry parallel: the Prosci ADKAR® Model (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement).
➤ Insight: For the last change you announced, which check has it reached today? If you cannot name the check, the change has been announced and left to chance.
✎ Reflection — The event and the transition

Write down one change your strategy requires of a named group. You will carry this change through the rest of the unit. On the day it was announced, how far through their own transition were the leaders, and how far were the people affected?

parts.title: 1.4 — The 3S Check: Shift, Stake, Step
content: 3S is the Mind check. It asks whether the people affected have understood the change as the leader intended it. Understanding is interpretation. Each person rebuilds the message through their own expertise, mental shortcuts, past experience and risk perception. The Functional Bias Problem from 1.1 applies in full: finance hears a cost decision, operations hears a process change, and the front line hears a judgement on how they have worked until now.

Leaders are poorly placed to judge this for themselves. After months inside a change, its logic feels obvious to them, and an obvious message feels like a clear one. The 3S Check replaces that feeling with a test. Mind passes when the people affected can say three things about the change in their own words.
Shift
“What is changing?”
What It Is

The Shift names the practice that ends and the practice that begins, for a named group, from a named date. It is concrete enough to be observed: someone watching the work could tell whether it is happening. A direction such as “more customer-focused” leaves every person to decide what it means, and each will decide differently.
Weak
“We are becoming more customer-focused.”
Clear
“From March, agents resolve complaints on the first call.”
Shows Up As
People describe the old practice under a new name • Different teams describe different changes
⚠ Execution: Chinese Whispers. The change mutates as it travels, and each function executes its own version.
➤ Leader’s move: State the Shift as from and to: what stops, what starts, for whom, from when.
Stake
“What do we gain if we change, and what do we lose if we stay as we are?”
What It Is

The Stake is why the change matters, and it has two sides. The gain says what the change is for. The loss says what standing still will cost. Both are needed, because people weigh a loss more heavily than an equal gain. A change described only by its benefits leaves the people affected holding the one visible loss: the practice they are asked to give up. Naming what is lost by staying put places a second loss on the scales. The Stake is stated in terms the affected group cares about. An enterprise benefit that never reaches their work reads as someone else’s reason.
Weak
“It supports our strategy.”
Clear
“We keep the customers who now leave after a two-day wait. If we stay as we are, we keep losing them.”
Shows Up As
“Because head office said so” • People can describe the change and cannot say what it is for
⚠ Execution: Compliance without conviction. The change is carried out while it is watched and set aside under pressure.
➤ Leader’s move: State the gain and the loss together, in the group’s own terms.
Step
“What do I do differently?”
What It Is

The Step is the person’s own part. It is said in the first person and is small enough to do next week. The Shift belongs to the organisation and the Step belongs to the person, so each role affected needs its own. A change with a clear Shift and no Step is understood as something that will happen to other people.
Weak
“Embrace the new process.”
Clear
“I decide on the call, within my limit.”
Shows Up As
“I am waiting to be told” • People agree with the change and carry on as before
⚠ Execution: Agreement without movement. The change is endorsed in meetings and absent from daily work.
➤ Leader’s move: Give each affected role its own Step, and ask people to say it back.
How to run the 3S Check
Write your own Shift, Stake and Step for the change.
Ask three people from the affected group to say theirs, without prompting.
Compare their versions with yours and with each other.
Reading the result
What you hear | What it tells you
The versions match. | Mind passes. Move to the Heart check.
Same Shift, different Stake. | People know what is changing and disagree on why. Restate the Stake in their terms.
Shift and Stake are clear, and there is no Step. | People see the change as someone else’s. Give each role its own Step.
Different Shifts. | Chinese Whispers. Return to one message, said in the same words by every leader.
Where a version differs from yours, the person’s own filter has reshaped it. The difference is information. It shows which part of the message to restate, and to whom.
The leader’s job at this check · Mind — Explain

The job: give people a version of the change they can repeat. State the Shift, the Stake and the Step in the same words each time, in every forum, until people can say them back. Repetition feels excessive to the leader long before the message has landed.
Complete when: three people from the affected group give the same Shift, Stake and Step.
Sounds like: “From March, complaints are resolved on the first call. We are losing customers who wait two days for an answer. Your part is to decide on the call, within your limit.”
⚠ When skipped: people fill the gap with their own version, and Clarification Debt builds: leadership time is spent re-explaining a change that was never understood the first time.
✎ Reflection — The 3S Check
Write the Shift, the Stake and the Step for the change you are carrying through this unit. Which of the three would your people find hardest to say back, and why?

parts.title: 1.5 — The SCARF Model: Five Triggers of Human Resistance
content: SCARF is the Heart check. When a trigger fires, a person who understands the change still withholds their energy from it.
Status
“Will this reduce my importance?”
Activated By
New leaders • New KPIs exposing performance • New systems shifting expertise • Changed reporting lines
Shows Up As
Defensive behaviour • Undermining decisions • Withholding information or cooperation
⚠ Execution: Political friction • Slowed decisions • Misalignment masked as professionalism
➤ Counter: Explicitly acknowledge existing credibility. Involve senior leaders in co-designing new structures.
Certainty
“Do I know what success looks like?”
Activated By
New goals • Ambiguous ownership • Changing metrics or timelines • Shifting review processes
Shows Up As
Repeated clarification requests • Delay disguised as “waiting for alignment” • Reversion to old habits
⚠ Execution: Loss of momentum • Paralysis under pressure • Risk avoidance
➤ Counter: Create visible milestones early. Give the brain enough structure to move without removing all ambiguity.
Autonomy
“Am I losing control of my work?”
Activated By
New systems • Standardised processes • Centralised decision rights • Increased oversight or reporting
Shows Up As
Passive compliance • Minimal effort delivery • Resistance through bureaucracy
⚠ Execution: Low engagement energy • Mechanical execution • Fragile performance
➤ Counter: Standardise the what and offer bounded choice on the how. Bounded choice preserves autonomy while honouring the mandate.
Relatedness
“Do I still belong here?”
Activated By
Team restructuring • New leaders or external hires • Cross-functional initiatives • Remote or hybrid shifts
Shows Up As
Silo behaviour • Reduced collaboration • Guarded communication
⚠ Execution: Trust erosion • Coordination breakdown • Rework and duplication
➤ Counter: Create visible connection rituals during transitions. People share resources only when they feel part of the tribe.
Fairness
“Is this being applied equitably?”
Activated By
Uneven workload • Selective enforcement • Inconsistent rewards • Unclear decision rationale
Shows Up As
Cynicism • Gossip replacing dialogue • Emotional withdrawal
⚠ Execution: Values misalignment • Morale drain • Cultural decay
➤ Counter: Explain rationale behind asymmetric decisions proactively. Transparency about trade-offs is perceived as fairness.
The leader’s job at this check · Heart — Involve

The job: give people a hand in shaping how the change lands. The leader decides what changes and opens up how it is done. Name plainly what people give up. Identify the live SCARF trigger and apply its counter. Involve their managers first, because managers carry the change into every team conversation.

Why it works: a part in the decision answers each trigger. Being consulted restores Status. Seeing the plan early restores Certainty. Choosing how restores Autonomy. Working on it together restores Relatedness. Hearing the reasons restores Fairness.
Complete when: the people affected can point to a part of the change they shaped.
Sounds like: “You know these calls better than I do. Where should the decision limit sit?”
⚠ When skipped: Silent Disengagement. People comply, do the minimum and wait to be chased.
✎ Reflection
Which SCARF trigger is most frequently activated in your organisation during strategy implementation? What is the observable evidence? What counter-strategy would address the root cause?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Which SCARF trigger is most frequently activated in your organisation during strategy implementation? What is the observable evidence? What counter-strategy would address the root cause?

parts.title: 1.6 — The STAT Check: Skill, Time, Authority, Tools
content: STAT is the Hands check. It asks whether people who understand a change and want it are able to carry it out on an ordinary working day. Mind and Heart sit inside the person. Hands sits largely in the conditions around the person, and those conditions are set by leaders.

This is the check most easily misread. A person who is unable to perform a change looks, from a distance, like a person who is unwilling: the new practice is late, partial or missing. A leader who reads that as resistance answers with more persuasion, when the gap is a missing decision right or a system that still fits the old way. STAT separates the two. Hands passes when all four elements are in place.
Skill
“Do they know how to do it?”
What It Is

Skill is the practised ability to do the new work to standard. It is built by doing the work with feedback. A briefing transfers information, and information becomes skill only after a person has performed the practice several times and been corrected.
Shows Up As
Errors and rework • Reliance on one or two experts • People reverting to the old method “to get it done”
⚠ Execution: Quality falls at the moment the change needs to prove itself, and the old way looks safer.
➤ Leader’s move: Teach, practise on real work and coach on the job. Pair the experts with the rest.
Time
“Do they have the hours to do it?”
What It Is

Time is the working capacity to perform the new practice properly. Most changes are added to a full day. When nothing is removed, the new work competes with the old, and the old work has the deadlines, the habits and the measures on its side.
Shows Up As
The new practice is done last • Done in a rush • Dropped on a busy day
⚠ Execution: The change is alive in quiet weeks and absent in busy ones.
➤ Leader’s move: Take old work away before adding new work, and say what stops.
Authority
“Are they allowed to decide and act?”
What It Is

Authority is the permission to decide and act as the change requires. Many changes move decisions closer to the customer or the front line. Until the limit of the new decision is stated, the safest course for the individual is to ask permission, and the decision travels back up to where it used to sit.
Shows Up As
Escalations • People ask permission for what the change asks them to do
⚠ Execution: The change runs slower than the practice it replaced, and leaders become the bottleneck.
➤ Leader’s move: Set the decision limit, state it openly, and back the first decisions made under it. The first decision that is overruled teaches everyone to keep asking.
Tools
“Do they have the systems and resources?”
What It Is

Tools are the systems, information and resources the new practice depends on. A practice has to be possible in the system people use every day. Where the system, the form or the budget still fits the old way, people build workarounds, and a workaround is the old practice surviving inside the new one.
Shows Up As
Spreadsheets beside the system • Manual steps • Requests waiting on another team
⚠ Execution: Two versions of the truth, extra effort and errors that stay hidden.
➤ Leader’s move: Provide access and budget before the start date, and retire the old form or route.
One missing element is enough to stop people who understand and want the change. Training closes a Skill gap. It leaves a Time, Authority or Tools gap exactly where it was.
The leader’s job at this check · Hands — Equip

The job: make the new practice possible on an ordinary working day. Run the STAT Check with the people affected, since they know what is missing. Supply it, and remove the old work, rules and approvals that stand in the way.
Complete when: a person can perform the new practice from start to finish without asking permission or using a workaround.
Sounds like: “What do you need from me to do this on Monday?”
⚠ When skipped: willing people fail, and their failure is read as resistance. Heart, which had passed, begins to fail as well.
➤ Insight: Which of the four is your organisation quickest to supply, and which is it slowest to grant?
✎ Reflection — The STAT Check
Run STAT for the change you are carrying through this unit. Which element is missing for the people it affects most? What is your evidence, and what is yours to supply?

parts.title: 1.7 — ACE-IT: The Observable Behaviour Standard
content: ACE-IT is the Habit check. These five behaviours are what hold a new practice in place.
A
Accountability
Definition
Taking full ownership for results. Acknowledging missteps and driving corrective action.
Desired Behaviour
Defines clear ownership • Acknowledges missteps • Holds self and others to measurable standards
✓ Observable: Commitments tracked • Reviews end with named owners • “We missed it, here’s the fix” language common
C
Commitment
Definition
Staying anchored to agreed strategic intent even when pressure rises. Following through despite discomfort.
Desired Behaviour
Aligns daily choices to long-term direction • Protects priorities from noise • Closes loops they open
✓ Observable: Strategic priorities stay consistent • Leaders decline non-strategic work • Promises kept visibly
E
Engagement
Definition
Actively involving self and others in sense-making, dialogue, and execution. Listening to understand.
Desired Behaviour
Invites participation and dissent • Connects roles to purpose • Creates two-way dialogue
✓ Observable: Team meetings are two-way • Feedback loops visible • People quote the shared “why”
I
Integrity
Definition
Acting consistently with values, facts, and truth — even when inconvenient.
Desired Behaviour
Says what is true, even when it is hard • Uses data to support choices • References values in trade-offs
✓ Observable: Evidence cited before decisions • Values referenced in hard choices • Teams trust word matches deed
T
Transparency
Definition
Making reasoning, progress, and constraints visible to all stakeholders. Sharing challenges openly.
Desired Behaviour
Communicates decisions with rationale • Documents choices and lessons • Shares progress including setbacks
✓ Observable: Dashboards updated regularly • Decisions logged and accessible • “No surprises” culture evident
How ACE-IT holds a new practice

Habit is the last check and the one asked earliest. The question is put before the change starts: how will the five behaviours hold the new practice in place? A change with no answer has no plan for the day after launch.
Behaviour | What it does for a new practice
Accountability | One named person owns the practice and its result.
Commitment | The practice is kept when pressure rises and the old way is quicker.
Engagement | People talk about how it is going and improve it together.
Integrity | Slips are reported as they are, and early.
Transparency | Its results are visible to everyone the change affects.
The leader’s job at this check · Habit — Reinforce

The job: make the new practice the expected practice. Show it yourself first. Notice it when it happens, recognise it by name and correct a slip early. Put it into the regular review so that it is asked about every time. What leaders ask about, people repeat. A practice that is never asked about is understood to be optional.
Complete when: the practice holds through a full review period with the leader absent.
Sounds like: “I saw you close that case on the call. That is the standard.”
⚠ When skipped: the old way returns under the first pressure, and the organisation concludes that the change was a phase.
✎ Reflection

If you audited your last leadership review against the ACE-IT behaviours — where would you find the biggest gap between the ideal and the observable? What one behavioural change would create the most impact?

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Does Heart & Mind Alignment Determine Execution Outcomes?
sections.sub: Within the Strategy2Results® process, Aligning Hearts and Minds functions as the ignition point of execution — the moment where strategy transitions from a document describing intent into a system capable of producing movement.
slo: Explain why shared understanding and commitment convert strategy into execution.
Distinguish commitment from compliance and explain why change delivers value only when it is adopted.

parts.title: 2.1 — The Ignition Point of Strategy Execution
content: A strategy document contains strategic potential. It articulates direction, ambition, and possibility. However, potential by definition represents energy at rest. For strategic potential to convert into kinetic energy — movement, execution, and results — human action must occur.

Execution begins the moment an individual decides: “This matters to me. I am willing to invest energy in making this succeed.” Until that moment occurs across the organisation, strategy remains theoretical. Aligning Hearts and Minds activates the human energy required to convert intention into action.
✎ Reflection
Think of a time when you personally chose to go beyond compliance and genuinely committed to a strategic direction. What caused that shift? What would it take to create that same shift in your team?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Think of a time when you personally chose to go beyond compliance and genuinely committed to a strategic direction. What caused that shift? What would it take to create that same shift in your team?

parts.title: 2.2 — Three Foundational Logics
content: I. Potential vs. Kinetic Energy Logic

A strategy document is strategic potential — energy at rest. For it to become kinetic energy, a human decision must activate it. Every day that decision is not made is a day strategic potential sits unused. The organisation does not move until people decide to move it.
II. Compliance vs. Commitment Logic
Compliance — Mind Only

People act because authority requires it. Produces visible output short-term. Requires continuous supervision. Creates hidden costs: leadership time consumed by follow-ups, decision-making slows as control increases. Mechanical and brittle.
Commitment — Mind & Heart

People act because they understand intent, believe the direction is meaningful, and feel personal ownership. Generates discretionary effort, adaptive problem-solving, resilience when conditions change. Execution continues when leaders are not present.
III. The Strategic Payoff of Alignment

When both cognition and emotion are aligned: people act with ownership, coordination improves across functions, and leaders spend less time correcting and more time advancing strategy. Aligning Hearts and Minds is the mechanical conversion point where strategic potential becomes strategic movement.
✎ Reflection
How much of your current leadership time is spent enforcing compliance? What is the opportunity cost of this?
prompts: ✎ Reflection How much of your current leadership time is spent enforcing compliance? What is the opportunity cost of this?

parts.title: 2.3 — Why Change Must Be Led: Installed and Adopted
content: 2.2 described a strategy as potential energy that a human decision converts into movement. A change follows the same logic. On the day it is installed, its value is still potential. The value is earned later, when people work the new way without being watched.
Installed
The new system, structure or KPI is in place, and people have been told.
Installation is a project outcome. It can be planned, funded and delivered on a date, and it is easy to report as success.
What you see: the launch is complete, the training register is signed and the dashboard is live.
What it yields: cost. The organisation has paid for the change and is still working the old way.
Adopted
People work the new way without supervision. The change has passed all four checks.
Adoption is a behavioural outcome. It arrives group by group, at the pace of each group’s slowest check, and no launch date can declare it.
What you see: the new practice holds on a busy day, people correct each other, and the old workaround has gone.
What it yields: value. The benefit the strategy counted on is being earned.
The adoption gap

The time between installed and adopted is the adoption gap. While it lasts, the organisation runs two practices at once: the new one it has built and the old one people still use. Supervision rises, because compliance has to be checked. The benefits counted when the strategy was approved remain unearned.

The gap also has a cost that outlasts the change itself. Every change that is installed and left unadopted teaches the organisation that a change can be waited out. The next change starts with less belief, and Heart is harder to pass.
The gap closes one check at a time. Compliance can install a change. Commitment is what carries it through to Habit, and adoption holds when leaders notice and reinforce the new practice.
Three signals a change is installed and awaiting adoption
Use of the new practice falls when the leader is absent.
Reports are complete and the result has not moved.
People call it “the new system” and describe their own work as unchanged.
Data: 81% of those who planned for reinforcement met or exceeded their project objectives (Prosci, Best Practices in Change Management, 12th edition).
✎ Reflection — Installed and adopted
Name one change in your organisation that is installed and still awaiting adoption. Which check did it fail: Mind, Heart, Hands or Habit? What has the adoption gap cost so far?

content: Click each COMPASS domain to explore the signal narrative and the facilitation question that drives early intervention.

The Signal Narrative

Clarity of Strategic Direction is whether people can describe the strategy in the same language, connect it to daily decisions, and hold it steady under pressure. When this signal flares: confidence in meetings, confusion in corridors. Priorities multiply and trade-offs are avoided.
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “Everyone has a different version of what we said.”
➤ Can every person in your leadership team describe the top three strategic priorities in the same order, using the same language? What would happen if you tested this now?
The Signal Narrative

Alignment is coordinated behaviour outside the room. Leaders declare alignment after a planning session and interpret absence of challenge as shared commitment. True alignment is only visible in behaviour. When this signal ignites, silos deepen and functions execute their own version of the strategy.
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We agreed on this — why is it not happening?”
➤ Where in your organisation do decisions made at the top not survive the journey to implementation? What sits between the decision and the delivery?
The Signal Narrative

Strategy fails in the gap between what leaders decide and what managers actually enforce, measure, and hold accountable. Management Discipline tells you whether the operating rhythm — reviews, escalation norms, accountability structures — is a genuine engine of delivery or an elaborate performance of oversight. When this signal flares, the same gaps appear in consecutive cycles and are explained and left uncorrected.
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We keep discussing the same issues with no resolution.”
➤ In your last three performance reviews, what was the single most recurring issue? Has it been resolved, or has it been re-explained?
The Signal Narrative

Organisations frequently approve strategies that their people are not yet equipped to deliver. This signal is particularly dangerous because it is slow-burning and easy to rationalise. Leaders attribute execution failures to process or strategy when the root cause is a capability system never designed to carry the weight being placed on it.
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We have the strategy but not the people to execute it.”
➤ If you had to deliver your strategy with the team you have today — which specific capability gaps would most limit you? When did you last name those gaps explicitly?
The Signal Narrative

An organisation’s true strategy is found in its budget. When this signal ignites, there is a visible gap between what leadership declares as strategic and what gets funded, staffed, and protected when decisions become difficult. Legacy spend continues by inertia while stated priorities are starved in practice.
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We say this is a priority but the resources tell a different story.”
➤ Look at your budget allocation. Does money follow the stated strategy? Where is the gap between declared priority and funded priority?
The Signal Narrative

The Sensing & Adaptation signal measures whether the organisation is genuinely learning from what is happening around it — or whether it is processing information selectively and defending existing plans. The deeper danger: when raising uncomfortable signals carries social cost, the organisation gradually loses its early warning system entirely.
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We knew this was coming, but we didn’t adapt fast enough.”
➤ What is one market or customer signal your organisation is receiving that is not yet reflected in your strategic plan? What would it take to act on it?
The Signal Narrative

A new strategy running through an old machine will always produce the same result. Systems & Execution asks: is the organisation actually built to deliver what it has committed to, in its architecture? Does the operating model match the strategic priorities?
Reflection Question
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “The structure is working against the strategy.”
➤ Is your current operating model designed for the strategy you have now — or for a strategy you had two years ago? What would redesigning the machine actually require?
✎ Reflection — COMPASS Diagnostic
Which domain did you rate highest risk? What is the observable evidence? Is it still a High Flammable or has it crossed to Burning Platform?

parts.title: 3.2 — From High Flammables to Burning Platforms
content: High Flammable Zone

Organisational leverage points. When alignment is strong: rapid clarity, coordinated effort, compounding momentum. When alignment is weak: distorted interpretation, defensive behaviour, multiplying friction.
✓ Early intervention stabilises the zone and converts it into a performance amplifier.
Burning Platform

What a High Flammable becomes when misalignment persists and crosses the escalation threshold. By this point, execution breakdown is visible and costly. Reactive interventions cost exponentially more than proactive alignment would have.
⚠ The same zone that was manageable as a leverage point becomes a crisis requiring systemic rebuilding.

parts.title: 3.3 — Change Readiness Across the Organisation
content: COMPASS shows where the organisation is exposed. Readiness shows how far each group of people has come through the 4 Checks for one specific change. The two are read together.

Readiness belongs to a group and a change together. The same group can be ready for one change and unready for another. The same change finds different groups at different checks, because it asks something different of each: one group gives up a decision, another gains one, a third carries on as before and feels overlooked.
How to run the scan
Name one change and list the groups it affects.
Run the 4 Checks for each group. Rate each check from 1 (fully in place) to 5 (missing).
Find each group’s first check that scores 4 or 5. Leadership effort for that group starts there.
Rating guide
Check | 1 · Fully in place | 3 · Partly in place | 5 · Missing
Mind · 3S | People give the same Shift, Stake and Step. | People give the Shift and differ on the Stake or the Step. | People give different versions of the change.
Heart · SCARF | People bring ideas and problems to the change. | People comply and stay quiet. | A SCARF trigger is live and resistance is open or hidden.
Hands · STAT | Skill, time, authority and tools are all in place. | One STAT element is missing. | Two or more STAT elements are missing.
Habit · ACE-IT | The practice holds when the leader is absent. | The practice holds when it is checked. | The new practice has not started, or the old one has returned.
Scores of 2 and 4 fall between these descriptions.
Worked scan · resolve complaints at first contact
Group | Mind | Heart | Hands | Habit | Start here
Contact-centre agents | 2 | 3 | 5 | 4 | Hands
Team leaders | 1 | 4 | 2 | 4 | Heart
Back-office specialists | 4 | 4 | 1 | 3 | Mind
Reading the scan
Contact-centre agents

Start at Hands. Agents understand the change and broadly accept it. They have no decision limit and no access to the refunds system. Further communication adds nothing for this group until authority and tools are in place.
Team leaders

Start at Heart. Team leaders understand the change best of all. It moves decisions from them to their agents, which fires Status and Autonomy. Until that is addressed, they are unlikely to coach agents to use the new authority, and the agents’ Hands gap will stay open.
Back-office specialists
Start at Mind. Specialists have the ability and have not been told what the change means for their own work. A strong Hands score has no effect while Mind fails.
One change, three groups, three starting points. A single plan written for every group serves one of them.
Three misreadings to avoid
Reading quiet as ready. A group that complies and stays silent scores 3 on Heart. Silence is the absence of information.
Reading a Hands gap as resistance. Late or partial practice looks the same whether people are unwilling or unable. Run STAT before concluding.
Averaging the scores. A group strong on three checks and failing one is stalled at that one. The first failing check decides, and an average hides it.
Readiness and COMPASS

Now place each group in its COMPASS zone from 3.1. Low readiness inside a High Flammable Zone marks where a change is most likely to cross the escalation threshold and become a Burning Platform. Those groups come first.

parts.title: 4.3 — Leading Change with One Voice
content: The 4 Checks describe what one group of people needs from one leader. Most changes reach a group through several leaders at once. People hear from their own leader, watch the others, and compare. Where the leaders differ, the group takes the difference as the real message.
In the Converging Zone, the leadership team makes four commitments that no single function can make alone. Each one protects a check. Expand each commitment.
One message
Protects Mind
What The Team Does

Every leader gives the same Shift, Stake and Step for each change. The Functional Bias Problem works on leaders first: each one translates the change through their own function before passing it on. The test is the 3S Check applied to the leadership team itself. Each leader writes the three for the same change, and the versions are compared before anyone speaks to their people.
⚠ When absent: Each function hears a different change, and the 3S Check fails across the organisation.
One example
Protects Heart
What The Team Does

Leaders show the ACE-IT behaviours the change needs before they ask for them. People read a leader’s diary, questions and decisions as the real message. A leader who asks for the new practice and keeps to the old one has told the organisation which of the two is safe.
⚠ When absent: People copy what leaders do and discount what leaders say.
One sequence
Protects Hands
What The Team Does

Leaders pool their changes and count how many land on the same group in the same period. The team then agrees the order and the pace. Each function sees its own change, and each change looks reasonable alone. The total load on a group is visible only when the team looks together, and Time is the first STAT element to give way under it.
⚠ When absent: One group is asked to absorb several changes together, and its willingness falls.

Data: Employees’ willingness to support enterprise change fell from 74% in 2016 to 43% in 2022, while planned changes per employee rose from two to ten (Gartner, reported in Harvard Business Review, 2023).
One owner
Protects Habit
What The Team Does

Each transition has one named leader who answers for adoption, through to Habit. The owner runs the 4 Checks, reports which check the change has reached, and stays with it after the launch, when attention moves to the next priority.
⚠ When absent: The change is installed and nobody answers for whether it is adopted.
Data: Projects with extremely effective sponsors were 79% likely to meet their objectives, against 27% with extremely ineffective sponsors (Prosci, Best Practices in Change Management, 12th edition).
✎ Reflection — One voice
Choose one group in your organisation. List every change the leadership team is asking of it this quarter. How many are there? Which of the four commitments is weakest in your team today?

Before strategy becomes operational activity, it must be interpreted, experienced, and accepted by the people responsible for carrying it forward. This unit establishes the human operating system that enables strategy to move from intention to execution. It equips leaders to lead people through the changes the strategy requires.
Critically examine how functional expertise, personality, cognitive bias and emotional conditions influence the interpretation of strategy.
Demonstrate shared strategic understanding and commitment across the leadership system.
Recognise the organisational conditions that strengthen or weaken strategic alignment.
